sam.name: Sam Park
sam.role: engineer (someone who designs and builds things to solve problems)

case.title: The Downhill Derby
case.hook: Hi again! Palmetto Beach is holding its first Downhill Derby. Kids built cars with no motors, and gravity (the pull that brings things down) pulls them down Dune Hill. My job is the hay bales at the finish line, so every car stops safely.

notice.head: PALMETTO BEACH DOWNHILL DERBY · RACE PROGRAM
notice.title: Saturday, 10 AM, at Dune Hill
rows: Low, Middle and High (the top of the hill)
Built by kids. No motors. Same size and weight rules.
Plan the hay bales. How long a stopping zone does each ramp need?
notice.line: Safety first: every car must stop safely in the hay.

stills.alt: A shiny red soap box derby car with four red wheels and an open seat.
A long, straight paved derby track running down a grassy hill between trees.
A small derby car crossing a finish line on a street, with soft padded barriers along both sides and people watching.

case.stillsCredit: Soap box derby racer (late 1960s design, a replica built by Bill Wrigley Jr.): Bill Wrigley (public domain). Derby Downs, the derby hill in Akron, Ohio: Troop330 (CC BY-SA 3.0). Soapbox race finish line in Differdange, Luxembourg: MMFE (CC BY-SA 4.0). All via Wikimedia Commons. Palmetto Beach, Dune Hill and the derby are made up for this lesson.
case.question: Which start ramp needs the longest stopping zone (the most hay bales), and why?
case.how: Find 4 clues as you work through the lesson. Then crack the case (solve it) at the top of the Assignment tab.

clues.t: The faster marble made the bigger crater. Faster means more energy, and more energy makes a bigger change.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 1: scrub the replay
clues.t: A moving object carries energy the whole time it moves. When it stops, the energy doesn’t vanish. It goes into what it hits, sound and a little warmth.
A harder pull sent the ball faster and higher. And a small fast baseball beat a big slow bowling ball. Speed matters a lot.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 4: build Dune Hill
clues.t: Higher start, faster car. The car from the High start pushed the hay bale the farthest.

solve.title: Which ramp needs the most hay?
solve.q: Which plan fits all four clues?

options.t: The Low ramp. Its cars are slowest, so they need the most help stopping.
options.why: Check Clue 4. Which start pushed the hay bale the farthest?

options.t: Whichever ramp has the heaviest car. Weight is all that matters.
options.why: Check Clue 3. Did the big, slow bowling ball win?

options.t: The High ramp. Its cars go fastest, so they carry the most energy and push the hay the farthest.
options.why: Case cracked! Faster cars carry more energy, so the High ramp gets the longest stopping zone. Now Sam can plan the hay bales.

options.t: Every ramp the same. The energy disappears when a car stops anyway.
options.why: Check Clue 2. Where does the energy go when something stops?

flick.title: The flour crater test
todo: Press on the marble and flick it DOWN with your mouse. (Or tap the buttons.)
Make one slow drop and one fast drop. Then compare the two craters.

why.t: A bowl-shaped dent made when something hits a surface. Flour shows the dent clearly.

flick.alt: A model: a marble held above a pan of flour, with a speed meter on the right.
flick.flickHint: Press on the marble and flick DOWN
flick.startLine: No drops yet. Flick the marble!
flick.midLine: That was a medium drop. Now try a very slow one or a very fast one.

opts.t: The faster marble carried more energy, so it made a bigger change.
The marble got heavier when I threw it hard.
opts.miss: It’s the same marble every time. What changed between your two drops?

opts.t: The flour was softer the second time.
opts.miss: The flour is smoothed the same way before every drop. What did YOU change?

photo.alt: The full Moon, covered with round craters.
photo.cap: Real craters! Rocks from space hit the Moon very fast and blasted out these bowls.
photo.credit: Full Moon: NASA Goddard / Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (public domain). Via Wikimedia Commons.

flick.win: Same marble, same flour. Only the speed changed, and the fast drop made the bigger crater. That’s your first clue!

replay.title: Scrub the replay
todo: Drag the slider (or press ▶) to step through the replay.
At each frame, tap EVERY place the energy is right now. Then press Check.

why.t: A video you can step through one frame (one still picture) at a time, like a sports replay on TV.

replay.alt: A model: a marble rolling toward a pencil lying on a table.
replay.ask: Where is the energy right now? Tap every place.

places.t: Spread out as a tiny bit of warmth

frames.cap: The marble rolls toward the pencil.
frames.hint: Is anything moving in this frame? A moving object carries energy, even before it hits anything.
frames.gone: The marble is rolling! Anything that moves has energy.
frames.ok: Yes! The marble carries energy the whole time it rolls, not just when it hits.

frames.cap: CLICK! The marble hits the pencil.
frames.hint: Three things happen at once: something is still moving, something starts to move, and something makes a noise.
frames.gone: Look and listen! Things are moving and making a sound.
frames.ok: Right! The marble passes its energy to the pencil, and some becomes the CLICK sound.

frames.cap: The marble stops. The pencil slides and rubs on the table.
frames.hint: Which thing is still moving? And rub your hands together fast. What do you feel?
frames.gone: The pencil is still sliding! Where is its energy?
frames.ok: Yes! The sliding pencil has the energy now, and rubbing on the table makes a tiny bit of warmth.

frames.hint: Nothing is moving now. But energy doesn’t vanish. Where did it spread out to?
frames.gone: Energy doesn’t vanish! The pencil rubbed the table and made a click. Where did that energy go?
frames.ok: Right! The energy didn’t disappear. It spread out as a tiny bit of warmth in the table and the air. It’s just too spread out to notice.

replay.q: When did the marble have energy?

opts.t: The whole time it was moving, even before the hit.
Only at the moment it hit the pencil.
opts.miss: Look at frame 1. The marble hadn’t hit anything yet. Was it moving?
A stopped marble isn’t moving. Look at frame 4 again.

replay.win: A moving object carries energy the whole time it moves. When it stops, the energy goes somewhere else. Clue 2!

pinball.title: Pinball power
todo: Pull the plunger: drag the red knob down, or tap a pull.
Predict which light the ball will reach. Then press Let go.

why.q: How does a pinball plunger work?
why.t: It’s a spring. Pull it back farther and it pushes the ball off faster. The table tilts uphill, so a faster ball climbs higher before it rolls back.

pinball.alt: A model pinball table tilted uphill, with a plunger lane on the right and three rows of lights.
pinball.predictQ: 2. Predict: which light will the ball reach?
pinball.wrongLine: Not what you predicted. That’s why scientists test!
pinball.needPred: Predict first: tap the light you think it will reach.
pinball.holdLine: Good pull! Now predict which light it will reach, then press Let go.

round2.title: Big and slow vs. small and fast
todo: Each ball rolls at a row of three wooden blocks. Which one knocks them over?
Tap your prediction, then run the test.
round2.q1: Your prediction: tap a ball. Then run the test.

balls.name: Bowling ball
balls.sub: 16 pounds, rolled gently at 1 mile per hour
balls.line: Bump. The blocks scoot a little and stay up.

balls.name: Baseball
balls.sub: 5 ounces, thrown at 60 miles per hour
balls.line: SMACK! All three blocks go flying.

round2.wrong: Surprise! Look at what happened to each row of blocks.
round2.needPick: Predict first: tap the ball you think will knock the blocks over.
round2.why: The bowling ball is about 50 times heavier. But the baseball is 60 times faster, and speed counts extra. The fast baseball carries about 70 times more energy!

opts.t: Speed matters a lot. A small fast ball can carry more energy than a big slow one.
Heavier things always have more energy.
opts.miss: Look at Round 2. Did the heavy bowling ball win?
Look at your three pulls. Which one climbed highest?

pinball.win: Faster ball, more energy. Even a small ball can beat a big one when it’s fast. Clue 3!

slowmo.afterText: film it with a super-fast camera
slowmo.title: A crash in slow motion
todo: Press Play in slow motion, or drag the slider one frame at a time.

why.t: A camera that takes thousands of pictures every second. A crash that is over in a blink can be seen step by step.

slowmo.alt: A real NASA high-speed photo sequence in 25 frames: a very fast ball hits a target, a bright flash, then a spray of hot gas and broken bits flies out and a crater forms.

caps.t: The hit! The super-fast ball flashes as it strikes.
Hot gas and bits of the target spray out.
A cone-shaped curtain of debris (broken bits) grows wider and wider.

slowmo.q: Where did the ball’s energy go?

opts.t: Into the flash, the flying debris and blasting out the crater.

opts.miss: Look at frames 2 to 16. Something huge happened when it stopped!
Watch the target. What changed there?

slowmo.credit: High-speed impact sequence: P. H. Schultz, Brown University, and the NASA Ames Vertical Gun Range (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons. The NASA Ames Vertical Gun Range in California can fire small balls at up to about 15,000 miles per hour.
slowmo.win: A small ball moving super fast carried enough energy to blast out a crater. Speed is powerful!

bulletin.afterText: film it with a super-fast camera
bulletin.title: The race-day announcer
todo: Press Play and listen. You can read along on the paper.
Tap the three phrases that tell how FAST a car is going. A place is not a speed!
lines: And they’re off in Heat 3! Car 7 starts at [[x:That’s a place on the hill. Listen for words about how fast a car goes.|the top of Dune Hill]]. Car 12 starts at the Low ramp.
Car 7 is [[fast|picking up speed]] all the way down!
The radar gun says [[mph|twenty-two miles per hour]]!
Car 12 rolls in [[slow|nice and slow]] and taps the hay bales.
Car 7 hits the bales with a big WHUMP! They slid back almost two feet. That’s a lot of energy!

dangers.does: Car 7 goes faster and faster downhill
a speed measured with a radar gun

bulletin.win: Faster car, bigger push. You heard the case in action!

drawpath.afterText: measure how far the car pushes the bale
drawpath.title: Build Dune Hill
todo: Press a flag on the tower (Low, Middle or High) and draw your hill down to the ground. Or tap the flag, then tap points.
Press Play. Then drag the red tape end to the bale (or tap the bale) to measure.
Do all three starts. Then drag each bar up to match your table.

why.q: How can a car go with no motor?
why.t: Gravity pulls it downhill. The higher it starts, the faster it’s going at the bottom.

drawpath.alt: A drawing area: a start tower on the left with Low, Middle and High flags, the ground, and a hay bale on the right.

lines.start: Start at a flag on the tower. Draw down to the ground.
lines.hint: Start at a flag on the tower
lines.tapMore: Now tap points down to the ground
lines.notDown: Keep going: bring your track down to the ground
lines.needStart: Start your track at one of the flags on the tower: Low, Middle or High.
lines.measureFirst: Measure the push first: drag the red tape end to the bale.
lines.stall: The car ran out of speed on a bump. A car can’t climb higher than where it started. Erase and try again.
lines.measure: Drag the red tape end to the front of the bale (or tap the bale).
lines.measureMiss: Line the tape end up with the front edge of the bale.
lines.recorded: Recorded! Press Erase my track and draw from another start.
lines.barMiss: Check each bar against your table. A bar turns green when it matches.

drawpath.chartQ: Build your bar chart: drag each bar up (or tap in the column) to match your table.
drawpath.q: What does your bar chart show?

opts.t: The higher the start, the faster the car, and the farther it pushed the bale.
All three starts pushed the bale the same.
opts.miss: Read your bars. Are they the same height?

opts.t: The Low start pushed it the farthest.

drawpath.win: Higher start, faster car, more energy, bigger push. Clue 4!

tool.name: Radar speed gun
tool.teaser: Clock a soccer ball, a bike, a derby car and a fastball.
tool.done: You clocked four speeds like a pro. A radar gun sticker is in your Field Notebook.

why.q: How does a radar gun work?
why.t: It sends out invisible radio waves. They bounce off a moving thing and come back changed. The faster the thing moves, the bigger the change, and the gun turns that into a speed.

radargun.title: Clock the speed
todo: When it’s inside the yellow beam, pull the trigger (or tap the beam).
radargun.alt: A police officer aims a radar gun out of a patrol car window.
radargun.cap: A real radar gun at work.
radargun.missLine: Nothing in the beam. Wait until it’s inside the yellow beam, then pull the trigger.

targets.name: Derby car (High start)
targets.note: Fast enough to need lots of hay!

q.q: Pretend the bike and the derby car weigh the same. Which one would push a hay bale farther?

opts.t: The derby car. It’s going faster.
opts.why: Right! Same weight, more speed, more energy. That’s why the High ramp needs the most hay.
We said they weigh the same. What’s different? Check your speeds.
Look at your speeds. Is one faster?

radargun.credit: A radar gun in use: U.S. Navy photo by Mass Communication Specialist 1st Class Hodges Pone (public domain). Via Wikimedia Commons.

q1.A: Food energy is stored. Think about the word “kinetic.” What does it go with?
q1.C: Sunlight is light energy. Which kind does every MOVING thing have?

q2.B: Think about your two flour craters. Did the slower drop make the bigger crater?
q2.C: Same marbles, different speeds. Did the pinball ball climb the same height for every pull?

q3.A: Cups can’t think! What was different about the ball?
q3.B: The ball stays the same weight. What changed between the rolls?

cer-4.label: your reasoning
cer-4.re: because|so |this shows|that shows|this means|that means|which means|proves|since

ans-2: Think about the flour craters and Pinball power. What happened when things went faster?
Use the word evidence: what did you SEE that proves it?
Try: Speed matters because ___. My evidence is ___.
ans-3: Think of something at home that moves: a ball, a door, a toy car.
What happens when it hits something fast? What do you see or hear?
Try: When I ___, it ___. That shows it had energy.
cer-4: First decide: does speed matter for energy?
Think about your craters, the pinball and your hay bale chart.
Try: I ___ because ___. One piece of evidence is ___. Another is ___.

planner.title: Your claim and two pieces of evidence

rows.label: 2. Pick two pieces of evidence from the lesson
options: The fast marble made a bigger flour crater than the slow one.
Pulling the plunger all the way sent the pinball higher than a little pull.
The small fast baseball knocked the blocks over. The big slow bowling ball didn’t.
The car from the High start pushed the hay bale farther than the car from the Low start.

planner.note: Tap your side and two facts. Then write your reasoning in your own words.

welcome.label: Welcome · the Downhill Derby
welcome.script: Hi again! It’s Sam. Palmetto Beach is having its first Downhill Derby! Kids built cars with no motors, and they race down Dune Hill. My job is the hay bales at the finish line. Read the race program. Which start ramp needs the longest stopping zone? Let’s find out!

warmup.label: Warm-Up · the flour crater test (Clue 1)
warmup.script: Let’s start with a crater test. Press on the marble and flick it down. Try a gentle drop first, then a really fast flick. Watch the crater grow. Then compare your two craters in the cards below.

vocab.label: Word Wall
vocab.notes: Walk slowly, then jog in place for “speed”; roll a ball for “motion”.

part1.label: Part 1 · scrub the replay (Clue 2)
part1.script: Here’s a replay of a marble rolling into a pencil. Drag the slider one frame at a time. At each frame, tap every place the energy is right now. Careful! The marble is moving before it hits anything.

part2.label: Part 2 · pinball power (Clue 3)
part2.script: Time for pinball! Pull the plunger back, then predict which light the ball will reach. Let go and watch it climb. Try a little pull, halfway, and all the way. Then comes Round 2: a big, slow bowling ball against a small, fast baseball.

part3.label: Part 3 · a crash in slow motion
part3.script: These are real photos from a NASA high-speed camera. Press Play, or drag the slider one frame at a time. Watch what a super fast ball does to the target.

explore.label: Part 4 · build Dune Hill (Clue 4)
explore.script: Now you design Dune Hill! Start at a flag on the tower and draw your track down to the ground. Press Play. Then drag the red tape to measure how far the hay bale slid. Do it from Low, Middle and High. Then build your bar chart.

assignment.label: Assignment · crack the case
assignment.script: Do you have all four clues? Crack the case at the top of this tab. Then answer two questions, fill in your speed table for Part C, and finish your C-E-R.

evidence.label: Use your evidence · CER
evidence.script: A classmate says speed doesn’t really matter. Hmm. Think about your craters, the pinball, and your hay bale numbers. Pick your side, tap two pieces of evidence in the planner, then explain how they prove your claim.

closing.label: Case closed
closing.notes: Celebrate; tease 19.02 (a fair test with trials).
closing.script: Case closed! Cars from the High start go fastest and carry the most energy, so they get the longest stopping zone. Next time we test it for real at Dune Hill: one change at a time, and lots of tries!

hlCoach.title: Highlight like a scientist
tips: Highlight key words, not whole paragraphs.
If everything is yellow, nothing stands out. Aim for a few words in each paragraph.
Look for words that are explained.
Bold words, and words followed by “means”, “is called” or a meaning in ( ), are often worth saving.
Look for answers to the Big Question.
Ask yourself: does this help me explain how speed and energy are connected?
“Because”, “so” and “first … then” show how ideas connect.
Yellow = important. Green = evidence I might use in my answer. Pink = something I wonder about.

practice.q: Practice: tap the 3 to 5 words that matter most in this sentence.
practice.text: The faster an object moves, the more energy it carries.
practice.model: A scientist might highlight “faster”, “more energy” and “carries”. Those words hold the big idea. Small words like “the” and “an” don’t carry the idea.

hlCoach.outside: This works in every subject. When you read anything, save the words that answer your question, and skip the rest.
